newsitem.title: USA: General says U.S. anti-missiles need closer watch.
newsitem.headline: General says U.S. anti-missiles need closer watch.

text.p: An urgent drive to develop U.S. anti-missile defenses has left one important missile program in serious trouble, and the general in charge says he is concerned others may stumble as well.
"I am concerned," Air Force Lt. Gen. Lester Lyles, commander of U.S. anti-missile programs, told reporters during a media tour of the Ballistic Missile Defense Organization research center here.

Lyles is under political pressure from Congress and President Bill Clinton to develop better anti-missile missiles quickly to shoot down enemy rockets as Patriot missiles did in the Gulf War -- and to be ready to defend the United States itself against a limited missile attack by 2003.

The anti-missile defenses are the remnant of President Ronald Reagan's 1983 Cold War dream of putting a shield over the entire United States to protect against the threat of thousands of Soviet missiles.

Dramatic television pictures of Patriots blasting Iraqi SCUDs in 1991, even though their success was overstated, built pressure to develop defenses at least against a limited missile strike by a potential enemy such as Iran or Libya.

The military is driving development of U.S. anti-missile missiles from the BMDO research center in this southern river valley. Lyles said the high-pressure drive has put one of the program's stars -- the battlefield THAAD missile meant to destroy enemy missiles at their highest arc in space -- into deep trouble after it failed all four flight tests so far.

Lyles said Army officials had to give Defense Secretary William Cohen options last Saturday ranging from revising the program to killing it, but he said the THAAD was too important to terminate. "I don't think you're going to see that happen."

He said the problem was that Lockheed Martin Corp. developed the missile so fast that it did not adequately test all the high-tech components in the nose that track a missile hundreds of miles out in space. A fifth test scheduled in July will be delayed at least until the end of the year, he said.
THAAD, which stands for Theater High Altitude Area Defense, is supposed to go into operation in 2004 but that is now in doubt, Lyles said.
He said the military has to sharpen management of other anti-missile programs including a defense for the entire United States to be sure they do not have the same trouble.

The Republican-controlled Congress approved an order for the U.S. missile defense in go into operation by 2003. But Clinton vetoed that, saying the millions of dollars should not be spent unless a specific threat emerges.

He responded to the Republican drive, however, by ordering accelerated development of the U.S. anti-missile defense so that a decision can be made in 2000 to build it in three years if there is a specific missile threat to America then.

In addition to the U.S. national defense, Lyles' command is developing at least a half dozen other battlefield missiles such as THAAD to defend U.S. troops and allies. The clearest success so far is an advanced Patriot built by Raytheon and Loral Vought Systems that is to go into operation in 1999.

Lyles called THAAD a lesson for other U.S. anti-missile programs of "the kind of things that a typical contractor might tend to overlook or not do or do less of when forced to address an aggressive schedule.

"We're going to have to learn because I don't think we're going to be allowed to back off of some of the requirements because of the urgency of the need," he said. "So we're going to have to take advantage and learn from past difficulties like THAAD."
